prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

NEW YORK (CNN) -- A construction company and three supervisors were indicted Monday on manslaughter and related charges in the deaths of two firefighters battling a 2007 blaze at the Deutsche Bank building in lower Manhattan. Firefighters Joseph Graffagnino, left, and Robert Beddia died in the Deutsche Bank building blaze. Prosecutors also reached an agreement with the city of New York requiring the implementation of new fire safety measures. "Our goal is to put in place procedures which will prevent a disaster of the magnitude of the Deutsche Bank fire and to make sure that firefighters are never again exposed to the risks they faced in that fire," Manhattan District Attorney Robert Morgenthau said. The indictments against the John Galt Corp., Jeffrey Melofchik, Mitchel Alvo and Salvatore DePaola also allege negligent homicide and reckless endangerment. The indictment is the result of an investigation into an August 18, 2007, blaze that consumed nine floors of the Deutsche Bank building. The building had been scheduled for demolition after being contaminated by debris, asbestos and other hazardous substances after the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center buildings. The two firefighters killed in the blaze -- Robert Beddia, 53, and Joseph Graffagnino, 33 -- were caught in a smoke-filled stairwell that prosecutors say was improperly blocked off by barriers erected to seal off floors being stripped of contaminants. In addition to the deaths of Beddia and Graffagnino, 105 other firefighters were injured combating the blaze. The agreement with the city of New York mandates the creation of a new civilian inspection unit at the city's fire department, the sole purpose of which will be to perform inspections at construction sites throughout the city. "The regulatory measures we have put in place and the additional reforms set out today are designed to prevent any firefighter again confronting the conditions that firefighters faced at the Deutsche Bank building that tragic day," New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg said in a written statement. The father of one of the firefighters killed in the blaze, Joseph Graffagnino Sr., said the indictments did not go far enough. "I don't understand if the [city] agency can't be indicted, why can't individuals be indicted who we already know should have been responsible for doing their jobs and did not do their jobs," he said to reporters. Graffagnino was referencing the lack of criminal charges brought against employees of the city fire department, the city's department of buildings and the building's landlord, the Lower Manhattan Development Corp.

NEW YORK (CNN) — A construction firm and three of its supervisors were charged Monday with manslaughter and other offenses connected to the deaths of two firefighters during a 2007 fire at Lower Manhattan’s Deutsche Bank building.

The victims, firefighters Robert Beddia and Joseph Graffagnino, died while responding to the blaze.

Prosecutors also entered into an agreement with New York City that calls for additional fire-safety safeguards. Manhattan District Attorney Robert Morgenthau said the objective was to establish procedures that would prevent another catastrophe on the scale of the Deutsche Bank fire and ensure firefighters are not again subjected to the dangers encountered there.

John Galt Corp. and supervisors Jeffrey Melofchik, Mitchel Alvo and Salvatore DePaola were indicted on charges that also include criminally negligent homicide and reckless endangerment.

The case followed an investigation into the August 18, 2007, fire, which spread through nine floors of the building. The structure was awaiting demolition because debris from the September 11, 2001, attacks on the World Trade Center had contaminated it with asbestos and other dangerous materials.

Beddia, 53, and Graffagnino, 33, became trapped in a stairwell filled with smoke. According to prosecutors, barriers intended to isolate floors undergoing decontamination had improperly obstructed the stairway.

Another 105 firefighters were hurt while fighting the fire.

Under the city’s agreement with prosecutors, the fire department must establish a new civilian inspection unit dedicated exclusively to examining construction sites across New York City.

In a written statement, Mayor Michael Bloomberg said the regulatory steps already adopted, along with the newly announced reforms, were intended to ensure that no firefighter would again face the conditions encountered at the Deutsche Bank building on that tragic day.

Joseph Graffagnino Sr., the father of one of the firefighters who died, argued that the indictments were insufficient. Speaking to reporters, he questioned why individuals could not be charged if the city agencies themselves could not be indicted, particularly when officials who were responsible for carrying out their duties had failed to do so.

His remarks referred to the absence of criminal charges against workers from the city fire department, the Department of Buildings and the property’s landlord, the Lower Manhattan Development Corp.

counterfactuals.output:
**NEW YORK (CNN) —** A Manhattan grand jury has indicted demolition contractor John Galt Corp. and three of its supervisors on manslaughter, criminally negligent homicide and reckless endangerment charges in connection with the 2007 fire at the former Deutsche Bank building in Lower Manhattan.

Firefighters Robert Beddia and Joseph Graffagnino were killed in the August 18, 2007, blaze at 130 Liberty Street, across from the World Trade Center site. More than 100 other firefighters suffered injuries, including smoke inhalation and heat exhaustion.

Prosecutors allege unsafe conditions inside the building contributed to the deaths. A stairwell that should have provided firefighters with an escape route had been blocked or sealed during demolition work, while portions of the building’s standpipe system — intended to deliver water to upper floors — were not functioning properly. Firefighters were forced to stretch hoses up the tower as smoke and flames spread through the structure.

The 41-story building had been heavily damaged and contaminated by dust and debris from the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. It was undergoing a complex decontamination and demolition process involving asbestos, lead and other hazardous materials when the fire broke out. Plastic sheeting and other containment materials used in the cleanup complicated visibility and movement inside the building.

The indictment accuses the company and supervisors of disregarding fire-safety requirements and creating conditions that placed workers and emergency responders at risk. The charges are allegations, and the defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty.

The fire also prompted New York City to tighten oversight of construction and demolition sites. The city introduced more frequent Fire Department inspections of high-rise projects, with particular attention to working standpipes, clear stairways, emergency access, fire watches and combustible materials. Officials also expanded coordination among fire, building and environmental agencies and required closer tracking of safety problems at active sites.

City leaders said the new measures were intended to prevent firefighters from again entering a building without reliable water supplies or unobstructed escape routes.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the legal developments following the August 18, 2007, blaze at the Deutsche Bank building in lower Manhattan, including who was indicted, the charges filed, the casualties, and the safety agreement reached between prosecutors and New York City.
counterfactuals.output:
After the August 18, 2007 fire at the former Deutsche Bank building at 130 Liberty Street—then being dismantled and decontaminated—a Manhattan grand jury brought charges stemming from the failure to maintain a working standpipe and other unsafe demolition conditions.

- **Casualties:** Firefighters **Robert Beddia** and **Joseph Graffagnino** died after becoming trapped in the smoke-filled building. More than 100 firefighters were injured or treated.
- **Defendants indicted:**  
  - **John Galt Corp.**, the demolition/abatement subcontractor  
  - Galt supervisors **Salvatore DePaola** and **Mitchel Alvo**  
  - **Jeffrey Melofchik**, the site-safety manager for construction manager Bovis Lend Lease
- **Charges:** The principal defendants faced **second-degree manslaughter**, **criminally negligent homicide**, and **second-degree reckless endangerment** charges. Prosecutors alleged that demolition work had cut or disabled the building’s standpipe and that repeated warnings and fire-safety requirements were ignored.
- **Disposition:** Alvo ultimately pleaded guilty to reckless endangerment and cooperated. In 2011, DePaola, Melofchik, and John Galt Corp. were acquitted of the homicide and reckless-endangerment charges after trial.

Separately, the Manhattan district attorney entered a **non-prosecution/safety-reform agreement with New York City**. In exchange for prosecutors not pursuing criminal charges against the city or its agencies, the city agreed to strengthen oversight of buildings undergoing construction, demolition, or asbestos abatement. The reforms included better coordination and information-sharing among the Fire Department, Buildings Department, and environmental regulators; more systematic inspections; clearer responsibility for checking standpipes and other fire-protection systems; and improved tracking and enforcement of fire-safety plans. The agreement reflected findings that fragmented city oversight had allowed hazardous conditions at the site to persist.

counterfactuals.output:
**Construction company, 3 supervisors indicted in fatal Deutsche Bank building fire**

**NEW YORK (AP)** — A demolition subcontractor and three construction supervisors were indicted Monday on manslaughter and other charges stemming from the 2007 fire at the former Deutsche Bank tower that killed two New York City firefighters.

The indictments charge the John Galt Corp. and supervisors Jeffrey Melofchik, Salvatore DePaola and Mitchel Alvo in connection with the Aug. 18, 2007, blaze at 130 Liberty St., across from the World Trade Center site. Firefighters Joseph Graffagnino, 33, and Robert Beddia, 53, died after becoming trapped in the smoke-filled building.

Prosecutors said workers had dismantled part of the building’s standpipe — the system firefighters use to carry water to upper floors — and failed to repair it or alert the Fire Department. Firefighters consequently had to stretch hoses up the tower’s stairways while flames spread through the contaminated, partially demolished structure.

“The deaths of Firefighters Graffagnino and Beddia were not the result of a tragic accident,” Manhattan District Attorney Robert Morgenthau said. “They were the foreseeable result of a series of reckless acts.”

The defendants faced charges including second-degree manslaughter, criminally negligent homicide and reckless endangerment. The indictments are accusations, and the defendants are presumed innocent unless convicted.

Mayor Michael Bloomberg called the charges “an important step toward accountability,” adding: “We will never forget Firefighters Joseph Graffagnino and Robert Beddia, who made the ultimate sacrifice while protecting our city.”

Graffagnino’s father, Joseph Graffagnino Sr., said the indictments were welcome but insufficient.

“It’s a start, but it doesn’t go far enough,” he said.

The elder Graffagnino believed responsibility extended beyond the subcontractor and on-site supervisors. He questioned why senior officials at construction manager Bovis Lend Lease and government agencies responsible for inspecting the troubled site were not criminally charged. The building had accumulated numerous safety violations, and inspections before the fire had failed to ensure that the standpipe was intact and operational.

For Graffagnino Sr., indicting only the company that performed the demolition work and several lower-level managers left unanswered questions about the broader chain of oversight — including who knew about the hazardous conditions and why work was allowed to continue.

The 41-story tower had been badly damaged in the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks and was being dismantled floor by floor when the fire erupted. Investigators said smoking materials likely started the blaze, but the disabled standpipe and other safety failures turned it into a deadly emergency.

counterfactuals.output:
## Deutsche Bank Fire Reshaped Construction-Site Safety in New York

The August 18, 2007, fire at the former Deutsche Bank building in lower Manhattan exposed serious weaknesses in the oversight of buildings undergoing demolition and environmental cleanup.

The vacant skyscraper at 130 Liberty Street, which had been badly damaged during the September 11 attacks, was being dismantled and decontaminated when fire broke out on an upper floor. Firefighters Robert Beddia and Joseph Graffagnino died while battling the blaze, and 105 firefighters were injured.

Firefighting operations were hampered by hazardous conditions inside the building. Smoke filled the stairwells, where containment barriers installed as part of the asbestos-abatement work obstructed movement and interfered with ventilation. Fire crews also encountered problems with the building’s standpipe system, limiting access to water on the upper floors.

Investigations found significant failures in inspections, interagency coordination and enforcement of fire-safety requirements at construction, demolition and abatement sites. The disaster prompted revisions to city regulations and closer coordination among the Fire Department, Buildings Department and other agencies.

One of the most consequential reforms was a mandate for a new civilian FDNY inspection unit focused on construction sites. The unit was intended to provide regular, specialized oversight of buildings undergoing construction, demolition or major alteration and to identify hazards before they could endanger workers or firefighters.

The fire’s aftermath became a turning point in New York City’s approach to construction-site fire safety, underscoring the need to keep stairways, standpipes and other emergency systems usable throughout complex building work.
